::: callout-note
## In this session you will learn to

1.  Explain that every column of a data frame is a **vector** with one type
2.  Use **vectorized** calculations and comparisons (and explain why `mutate()` needs no loop)
3.  **Subset** vectors and data frames with base R (`[ ]`, `$`, `[[ ]]`) and compare it with `filter()`/`select()`
4.  Describe **tidy data**, and reshape between wide and long with `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`

**Before you start:** open the workshop folder in Positron (**File → Open Folder...**) and open `scripts/Session 4 - Data Structures_STUDENT.R`. This session starts from the finished data of Session 3: `processed_data/combined_linelist.rds` and `processed_data/measles_final.rds`. Missed Session 3? Ready-made copies of both files are already in `processed_data/`.
:::

Sessions 1–3 used tidyverse functions that hide how R stores data. Today you look under the hood: vectors and vectorization explain *why* `mutate()` works on a whole column at once, base-R subsetting is everywhere in help pages and other people's code (and you will need it to write functions in Session 8), and reshaping is needed for many summaries and plots.

# Part 2: Vectors and types

A **vector** is a set of values of the **same type**. Every column of a data frame is a vector. `$` pulls one column out:

```{r}
ages <- linelist$age_years
head(ages)
length(ages)
```

`length()` tells you how many values a vector has: 6451, one per row of `linelist`.

## The main types

| Type        | Example                   | `class()` says |
|-------------|---------------------------|----------------|
| Number      | `38.5`, `2`               | `"numeric"`    |
| Text        | `"male"`, `"Recover"`     | `"character"`  |
| TRUE/FALSE  | `TRUE`, `FALSE`           | `"logical"`    |
| Date        | `as.Date("2014-05-13")`   | `"Date"`       |
| Factor      | categories with an order  | `"factor"`     |

```{r}
class(linelist$age_years)
class(linelist$gender)
class(linelist$onset_date)
```

## One type per vector

If you mix types, R converts everything to the most flexible type — usually text. This is why a single "unknown" turned the whole `age` column into text in Session 1:

```{r}
c(1, 2, "unknown")
c(1, TRUE, FALSE)    # TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0
```

## Missing values spread

Any calculation with `NA` gives `NA`, unless you tell R to skip them:

```{r}
mean(c(38, 39, NA))
mean(c(38, 39, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (3 min): types in the measles data

Use `class()` on `measles$age_years`, `measles$vaccinated`, and `measles$report_date`, and `length()` on `measles$temp_c`.

✅ **Check:** "numeric", "character", "Date", and 1163

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
class(measles$age_years)
class(measles$vaccinated)
class(measles$report_date)
length(measles$temp_c)
```

Ages are numbers, vaccination status is text, and the report date is a real date. The length is 1163 — one value per row, because a column is just a vector.
:::
:::

# Part 3: Vectorization

R does most calculations on **every element of a vector at once**. No loop needed:

```{r}
temps_c <- c(36.8, 38.5, 40.1)
temps_c * 9 / 5 + 32
```

That is exactly what happens inside `mutate()`: the calculation runs on the whole column.

```{r}
# Weight in pounds for every patient, in one line
head(linelist$wt_kg * 2.2)
```

## Comparisons are vectorized too

A comparison gives a **logical** vector, one TRUE/FALSE per element:

```{r}
temps_c > 38
```

TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, so:

-   `sum()` of a comparison **counts** the TRUEs
-   `mean()` of a comparison gives the **proportion** that are TRUE

```{r}
sum(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE)    # how many patients had temp above 38
mean(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE)   # what proportion
mean(linelist$fever == "yes")            # proportion with fever
```

You will use this trick again in Session 5: `mean(fever == "yes") * 100` inside `summarise()` gives the percentage with fever in each group.

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): vectorized calculations

a)  Convert `measles$temp_c` to Fahrenheit and look at the first values with `head()`
b)  Count the cases with a temperature of 39 or more: `sum(... >= 39)`
c)  Find the proportion of cases who were vaccinated: `mean(... == "Yes")`

✅ **Check:** a) starts 100.94, 101.12 b) 565 c) 0.238

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
head(measles$temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32)    # a)
sum(measles$temp_c >= 39)            # b)
mean(measles$vaccinated == "Yes")    # c)
```

565 cases had a temperature of 39 °C or more, and 23.8% of cases were vaccinated. No `na.rm = TRUE` is needed here because `temp_c` has no missing values after cleaning.
:::
:::

# Part 4: Subsetting with base R

**Subsetting** means pulling out part of a vector or data frame. The tidyverse does this with `filter()` and `select()`; base R uses square brackets. You will see base R in help pages, older code, and when writing functions (Session 8).

## Vectors: `x[ ]`

```{r}
temps_c[1]            # first element
temps_c[c(1, 3)]      # first and third
temps_c[-1]           # everything EXCEPT the first
temps_c[temps_c > 38] # elements that meet a condition
```

## Data frames: `df[rows, columns]`

Inside the brackets, **rows come first, then columns**, separated by a comma. Leave one side empty to keep everything:

```{r}
linelist[1:3, c("case_id", "age_years", "outcome")]   # rows 1–3, three columns
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
linelist[1:3, ]                                       # rows 1–3, all columns
linelist[, "age_years"]                               # all rows, one column
```

## One column: `$` and `[[ ]]`

```{r}
linelist$hospital_name[1:3]        # $ with a name you type
linelist[["hospital_name"]][1:3]   # [[ ]] with a name in quotes — useful inside functions
```

## Conditions

```{r}
# Mean temperature of patients who died
mean(linelist$temp[linelist$outcome == "Death"], na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: callout-warning
## Base R and missing values

```{r}
nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40, ])   # 244 rows?!
nrow(filter(linelist, temp > 40))     # 93 rows
```

Base R returns an **extra row of NAs for every missing temperature** (151 of them). `filter()` drops rows where the condition is NA. With base R, add `& !is.na(temp)`, or just use `filter()`:

```{r}
nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40 & !is.na(linelist$temp), ])   # 93: fixed
```
:::

## Base R vs tidyverse

| Task | Base R | Tidyverse |
|------|--------|-----------|
| Rows that meet a condition | `df[df$age > 40, ]` | `filter(df, age > 40)` |
| Some columns | `df[, c("a", "b")]` | `select(df, a, b)` |
| One column as a vector | `df$a` or `df[["a"]]` | `pull(df, a)` |
| First rows | `df[1:5, ]` | `slice(df, 1:5)` or `head(df, 5)` |

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Forgetting the comma: `df[1:3]` picks **columns** 1–3, not rows!
-   Base R adds a row of NAs for every NA in the condition (see the box above). Add `& !is.na(...)`, or use `filter()`.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): subsetting the measles data

With base R,

a)  Show rows 1–5 of the `patient_id` and `temp_c` columns of `measles`
b)  Find the mean temperature of children who died (`outcome == "Died"`)
c)  Count the cases aged 15 or older with `nrow(measles[...])`, then with `filter()`. Why are the answers different? Fix the base R version.

✅ **Check:** a) the first ID is MS-0931 b) 38.75 c) 225 vs 196 (29 missing ages)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
# a)
measles[1:5, c("patient_id", "temp_c")]

# b)
mean(measles$temp_c[measles$outcome == "Died"])

# c)
nrow(measles[measles$age_years >= 15, ])
nrow(filter(measles, age_years >= 15))
nrow(measles[measles$age_years >= 15 & !is.na(measles$age_years), ])   # fixed
```

Base R gives 225 rows because it adds a row of NAs for each of the 29 cases with a missing age. Adding `& !is.na(measles$age_years)` gives 196, the same as `filter()`.
:::
:::

# Part 5: Tidy data and `pivot_longer()`

## Tidy data

Data is **tidy** when:

1.  Each **variable** is a column
2.  Each **observation** is a row
3.  Each **value** is a cell

The tidyverse works best on tidy data. But "observation" depends on your question. Our symptoms are in **wide** format — one column per symptom:

```{r}
linelist %>% select(case_id, fever:vomit) %>% head(3)
```

To count or plot **all** symptoms together, we want **long** format: one row per patient *per symptom*.

## `pivot_longer()`: wide → long

```{r}
symptoms_long <- linelist %>%
  select(case_id, fever:vomit) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = fever:vomit,   # the columns to stack
    names_to  = "symptom",     # new column for the old column NAMES
    values_to = "present"      # new column for the VALUES
  )

head(symptoms_long)
nrow(symptoms_long)   # 6451 patients × 5 symptoms
```

`fever:vomit` means "every column from fever to vomit".

Now one `count()` answers "how many patients had each symptom?":

```{r}
symptom_counts <- symptoms_long %>%
  filter(present == "yes") %>%
  count(symptom)

symptom_counts
```

And it's ready to plot (a preview of Session 6):

```{r}
ggplot(symptom_counts, aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(symptom, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Patients reporting each symptom", x = "Number of patients", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): measles symptoms long

Select `patient_id`, `fever`, and `rash` from `measles`, then `pivot_longer()` the two symptom columns. `count()` `symptom` and `present`.

Pattern: `pivot_longer(cols = c(COLUMN_1, COLUMN_2), names_to = "symptom", values_to = "present")`

✅ **Check:** 2326 rows (1163 × 2); fever yes 1064, rash yes 976

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_symptoms <- measles %>%
  select(patient_id, fever, rash) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(fever, rash),
    names_to  = "symptom",
    values_to = "present"
  )

nrow(measles_symptoms)
measles_symptoms %>% count(symptom, present)
```

Each of the 1163 cases now has two rows, one for fever and one for rash, so there are 2326 rows. One `count()` gives the yes/no totals for both symptoms.
:::
:::

# Part 6: `pivot_wider()`

The opposite: long → wide. Most useful for **tables people read**. `count()` gives long output:

```{r}
linelist %>% count(hospital_name, outcome)
```

`pivot_wider()` spreads it into a cross-table:

```{r}
linelist %>%
  count(hospital_name, outcome) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = outcome,   # values that become the new column NAMES
    values_from = n          # values that fill the cells
  )
```

`values_fill = 0` puts 0 instead of NA where a combination doesn't exist.

::: callout-note
## Long for R, wide for people

Keep data **long** for analysis and plotting; make it **wide** at the end for a table someone will read.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): a district × vaccination table

`count()` `district` and `vaccinated` in `measles`, then `pivot_wider()` so each vaccination status is a column.

✅ **Check:** 6 rows (5 districts + Unknown); North has No 205, Unknown 49, Yes 88

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles %>%
  count(district, vaccinated) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = vaccinated,
    values_from = n
  )
```

The values of `vaccinated` (No, Unknown, Yes) become the column names, and the counts fill the cells: one row per district.
:::
:::

::: callout-tip
## ⭐ Bonus

1.  Turn the district × vaccination table into **percentages**: before `pivot_wider()`, `group_by(district)` and add `mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))`, then use `values_from = pct`.
2.  `pivot_longer()` the `fever` and `rash` columns, keep the "yes" rows, and plot the count of each symptom by `vaccinated` with `geom_bar(position = "dodge")`.
3.  Brought your own data? Is it wide or long? Reshape it the other way.

The code for 1 and 2 is in the solutions file.
:::

# Key points

-   Every column of a data frame is a **vector**, and every vector has **one type** — check it with `class()`. Mixing types turns everything into text.
-   Any calculation with `NA` gives `NA` unless you add `na.rm = TRUE`.
-   Calculations and comparisons are **vectorized**: they run on every element at once, which is why `mutate()` needs no loop.
-   `sum()` of a comparison **counts** the TRUEs; `mean()` gives the **proportion**.
-   Base R subsets with `x[ ]`, `df[rows, columns]`, `df$col`, and `df[["col"]]` — but watch out for the extra NA rows that `filter()` would drop.
-   Tidy data has one variable per column and one observation per row. `pivot_longer()` makes data long (for analysis and plots); `pivot_wider()` makes it wide (for tables people read).

**Next: Session 5 — Summarizing.** We summarize data with `count()`, `group_by()` + `summarise()`, and `tabyl()`, and build a publication-ready Table 1.
